primitives.name: Temporal Pacing Optimization
primitives.verbatim_quote: In a race they should stick to their own pace, particularly in the first quarter; but when they reach the last quarter, it is time to begin to pick up the leader, and in the stretch run the last bit out.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'t': 'time in seconds', 'v(t)': 'velocity function in m/s', 's(t)': 'distance function in meters'}
primitives.assumptions: Constant acceleration within segments, linear velocity profile in early stages, exponential deceleration in final segment.

layer2.mapping: State transition from conservative pacing to aggressive sprinting based on elapsed time and distance covered.
layer2.telemetry: Time-to-distance ratio deviation from optimal pacing curve.

primitives.name: Opponent Tracking Kernel
primitives.verbatim_quote: If you know there is a great runner in your race, it is often good policy to pick him out and dog his tracks, unless you feel that he is setting an unusual pace purposely.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'d_{rel}(t)': 'relative distance to opponent in meters', 'v_{rel}(t)': 'relative velocity in m/s'}
primitives.assumptions: Opponent maintains consistent velocity profile, relative motion is planar.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to Kalman filter tracking in dynamic environments with noisy observations.
layer2.telemetry: Deviation from expected opponent trajectory over time window.

primitives.name: Burst Mechanics Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: If you find him going slow of your gait, you had better move up rather than let him keep you back, because he can probably make too long a burst for you later in the race.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'a_{max}': 'maximum acceleration in m/s^2', 't_{burst}': 'duration of burst in seconds', 'v_{peak}': 'peak velocity during burst in m/s'}
primitives.assumptions: Acceleration phase is instantaneous, burst duration is bounded.

layer2.mapping: Dynamic threshold-based decision engine for initiating high-intensity bursts.
layer2.telemetry: Ratio of actual vs. predicted burst timing efficiency.

The temporal pacing optimization primitive formalizes this through a piecewise velocity function where early segments maintain baseline performance while late segments allow for burst-like acceleration. This is modeled mathematically as a composite function of time-dependent velocity profiles, constrained by physical limits of human biomechanics. The opponent tracking kernel introduces a second-order control loop where the athlete's position relative to competitors is continuously monitored and adjusted. This creates a feedback system akin to a control theory problem with multiple inputs—pace, distance, and competitor behavior. The burst mechanics model then acts as a trigger mechanism, determining optimal moments for high-intensity effort based on relative positioning and anticipated competitor behavior. These primitives form a hierarchical decision-making architecture where each layer refines the previous one, creating a robust framework for race execution.
